topic.title: The bank sold you the EMI, not the flat
topic.claim: A 25-year home loan doesn't make the flat affordable; it makes the EMI affordable, and that is the only number anyone shows you.
topic.moment: The builder's sales person punches numbers into a calculator and says 'sirf ₹48,000 a month'.

turn.believed: A longer loan is a relief because the monthly payment is smaller.
turn.actually: The longer tenure keeps the price high and you pay a big chunk more in interest over the years.

topic.feeling: I'll be paying for this flat till I'm almost retired.
topic.villain: Loan tenures stretched to fit high property prices
topic.because: Builders and banks both win when the conversation is about the monthly figure. The total cost is hidden behind a smaller, friendlier number.
topic.payoff: Ask for the total you will pay over the loan, not the EMI. Then decide.
topic.behaviour: Buyers pick the longest tenure to fit EMI within salary; sellers pitch only the EMI.
topic.mechanism: A smaller monthly number makes a high total price easy to say yes to.
topic.group: First-time homebuyers in their late 20s and early 30s
topic.send_to: The couple currently visiting sample flats on weekends.
topic.why_now: Flat prices keep rising, so tenures get longer to keep the EMI looking fine.
topic.needs_facts: A simple worked example: total interest paid on a typical home loan at current rates over 20 vs 25 years.

score.why: A long loan makes the EMI affordable, not the flat; it hits the weekend flat-visit couple.

reader.point: Long home loans make the monthly EMI look affordable but cost you far more in total interest, so you should ask for the total amount payable before buying a flat.
reader.reason: Sellers, banks and builders all benefit when buyers focus only on the EMI and not the total, and flat prices have outrun salaries so long loans feel necessary.

sources.fact: For a ₹50 lakh loan at 8.50%, stretching the tenure from 10 to 25 years cuts the EMI from ₹62,024 to ₹40,261. Total interest rises from ₹24.43 lakh to ₹70.78 lakh, so the 25-year loan costs far more overall.
sources.stance: supports the claim that a long tenure shrinks the EMI while inflating total cost. It is a broker's explainer, not a primary source, and it says nothing about builders or banks pushing the EMI figure.
sources.excerpt: Tenure: 25 years | Monthly EMI ₹40,261 | Total Interest Paid ₹70.78 lakh (table row; the 10-year row shows ₹62,024 and ₹24.43 lakh, the 30-year row shows ₹38,446 and ₹88.41 lakh). "Delivers the lowest possible monthly installment by utilizing the maximum house loan tenure available". "Greatly inflates your total interest burden over time." "it often results in significantly higher total interest payments."

sources.fact: When rates rose in 2022, lenders kept EMIs roughly steady and lengthened tenures, so 20-year home loans ran to 24 years. Borrowers ended up paying many more EMIs.
sources.stance: supports the claim that the EMI is the number that gets managed while the tenure and total cost quietly grow. It does not address sellers' pitches.
sources.excerpt: "the 20-year mortgages now last 24 years." For a Rs50 lakh loan taken in April 2019, the "initial term would be extended from 20 years to 22 years, 10 months." The borrower would "have to pay 60 more EMIs than they originally would have."

sources.fact: Knight Frank's H1 2026 index measures affordability as the share of household income that goes to home loan EMIs. It treats 50% or less as affordable, and six of the eight largest markets met that threshold.
sources.stance: neutral. The industry's own affordability yardstick is an EMI-to-income ratio, which fits the claim that EMI is the headline metric. The page does not discuss total cost or tenure, and it does not say who benefits from the focus on EMI.
sources.excerpt: "The index calculates the share of household income required to service home loan EMIs." "Home affordability remained within the 50% threshold in six of India's eight largest residential markets"

cover.headline: A 25-year loan makes the [monthly EMI] affordable, not the flat
cover.sub: The monthly number is the only one anyone shows you.

paragraphs: A 25-year home loan doesn't make the flat cheaper. It only makes the monthly EMI smaller.
slides.why_swipe: If the EMI fits my salary, what's the problem?

paragraphs: And the EMI is the only number anyone will show you.
The total you pay over 25 years never comes up, and that's the number that would make you think twice.
The sales guy asks your combined take-home before he asks which floor you like. Then he taps his calculator and turns it to you. "Sirf ₹80,000 a month, sir."
slides.why_swipe: What did the calculator leave out?

paragraphs: Take a ₹1 crore loan at 8.5%. Over 10 years, the EMI is ₹1,24,048 and the interest is ₹48.86 lakh.
Stretch it to 25 years. The EMI drops to ₹80,522. The interest jumps to about ₹1.42 crore.
slides.why_swipe: So what does that relief really cost?

paragraphs: You save a good chunk every month.
But the longer loan costs about ₹93 lakh more in interest. That's the extra you pay for the smaller EMI.
You borrowed ₹1 crore. You pay back ₹1.42 crore in interest alone.
slides.why_swipe: Why does nobody bring this up?

paragraphs: So the calculator stops at the monthly number.
As long as the EMI fits your salary, the builder never has to drop the price of the flat. The bank collects interest for 25 years.
Both win while you look only at the EMI.
slides.why_swipe: So why not just take a shorter loan?

paragraphs: And a shorter loan is often not a real choice. Flat prices left salaries behind years ago. That bigger EMI is more than many couples take home in a month.
Sign young, and you're still paying in your fifties.
slides.why_swipe: What do you do at the next site visit?

paragraphs: Next weekend, when the calculator turns towards you, ask him to press one more button. Total amount payable.
Then watch how long he takes to find it.

end.save: Open this again before your next weekend at a sample flat.
end.send: Send to the couple spending every Sunday in sample flats and comparing EMIs on the drive home.
end.promise: How things really get sold to us.

draft.alt_text: A text carousel arguing that a 25-year home loan makes the monthly EMI smaller but not the flat cheaper, and that the EMI is the only number buyers are shown. It shows a typical site visit where the salesperson pitches only the monthly figure, compares a ₹1 crore loan at 8.5% over 10 and 25 years, works out that the longer loan costs about ₹93 lakh more in interest, explains that the builder keeps the price high and the bank earns interest while buyers look only at the EMI, notes that a shorter loan is often out of reach and a long loan runs into the buyer's fifties, and ends by telling buyers to ask for the total amount payable.
